adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Turkey - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's Turkey country overview is the framework every Turkish province, Niğde included, stands under: homosexuality has been decriminalised since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised, and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military: the armed forces' health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and those receiving an 'unfit report' may face later discrimination in public life. Pride events have been banned in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions, and ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Turkey 47th out of 49 countries. A court case to close Lambda Istanbul was overruled by the Constitutional Court, and a February 2026 press report of draft legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison was not included in the 12th judicial package, whose passage removed provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible. The page carries no Niğde-specific content, but under the lane spec a national-framework document stays on a province record when that framework is what the visitor stands under and no province-specific source covers the point.

adds.title: Türkiye - Amnesty International country report (Report 2025/26)
adds.summary: Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26), which covers the national situation applying to every province including Niğde: in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end, and in December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association after ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. Amnesty records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025 - an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible - but they were ultimately not submitted to parliament.
